text:
THE SAVOY MALE AND FEMALE COLLEGE  217

ROBERT ROBINSON HALSELL

    I spoke briefly on the life of Mr. Halsell at the time of the laying of the cornerstone of this building, and wish to repeat on this occasion what I said about him then, since some reference to him seems most appropriate.

    There are four or five outstanding facts about Mr. Halsell which I especially remember, the first of which is that he was a great disciplinarian. Eight o'clock was the opening hour for our morning exercises, not 8:00 nor 8:10, or any later period, but woe to any student who came in after the opening bell rang. Every morning about 7:50 or 8:00 o'clock, when Mr. Halsell would come into the room and begin calling and checking exercises, you were supposed to have pencil and paper ready and when to copy the exercises, and when after he had given them, they were handed in at the close of morning exercises and a grade was given for it, and those who failed to submit a report were also called to account. These morning exercises were in keeping his record keeping so accurate and complete as one of the greatest I have ever known.

    I want to second, he a great humanitarian. Every student felt free to take his troubles to him, and when some of the boys could not find the money to meet tuition, those who had money were not made aware of it, by what he called "Back halls." I do not know whether he charged anything or the use of these back halls. I know Mr. Halsell never refused to allow any boy or any girl without money from what I have not done from their own to come to his school.

    Third, he was a real Christian gentleman, a real Christian gentleman, and when you can say that about any man you are saying a lot. He was a man well liked of the community, and I do not recall that I ever heard of anything but an unbecoming conduct on the school premises or among his students at any time.

    Fourth, he was a great educator. He knew how to teach, and teaching in a small school is a very much harder job than teaching in a large school. The small school teacher must know how to teach. The test of Mr. Halsell's teaching was that his students got results. I believe that it is safe to say that a greater number of students and a more self-reliant boy or girl who ever went to Mr. Halsell arose out in life than any boy or girl I have ever known.

    Fifth, Mr. Halsell was an ideal family man. He reared a family in a little town of Savoy that was one of those outstanding families. I knew all of his children, and when you just say something to the son or those two daughters who are reading on the platform and hear them extol the virtues of their father.
notes: This section is a tribute to Robert Robinson Halsell, delivered by Gus W. Thomasson.
